nodes.title: The RAG Pipeline
nodes.tease: Most RAG failures happen before the model sees a single token. Which stage is quietly to blame?

primer.problem: A law firm holds millions of documents, far more than a language model can read in one request. Lawyers want answers drawn from their own contracts and emails, with a pointer to the exact page, not from whatever the model half-remembers from its training data.
primer.picture: Think of it as Elasticsearch sitting in front of a chatbot. **Offline**, like a Kafka consumer, each new document is cut into short passages, each passage becomes a list of numbers that captures its meaning, and both go into an index. **Online**, the question is turned into numbers the same way, the closest passages are fetched, and only those are pasted into the prompt with their ids. The model answers from them and cites the ids; your code then checks every cited id was really sent.
primer.sketch:
OFFLINE (when a document arrives)     ONLINE (per question)
document -> split into chunks         question -> embed
         -> embed each chunk                   -> search index -> top chunks
         -> store in index ------------------> prompt with chunk ids -> LLM
                                               -> check cited ids -> answer

terms.def: Fetching relevant passages from your own documents first, then asking the model to answer using only those passages.
A short passage, typically a few hundred words, cut from a longer document so it can be searched and quoted on its own.
A fixed-length list of numbers a model produces for a piece of text, so texts with similar meaning get similar numbers.
The provider stores an unchanged prompt opening, such as a whole document set, so repeat requests reusing it cost less and run faster.
Anthropic's technique of adding a short model-written sentence of context to each chunk before it is embedded and keyword-indexed.
The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens (word pieces), that a model can read in one request.
AWS's managed RAG service: it ingests documents from S3 and other sources, chunks and embeds them, and serves search and cited answers.

inPractice.setting: A regional tax authority's staff assistant over 50,000 guidance notes and rulings
inPractice.story:
Caseworkers answered taxpayer letters by digging through a share full of guidance notes and rulings. Finding the paragraph that settled a VAT question could take forty minutes, and the generic chatbot IT trialled answered fluently from its training data, quoting rules that had changed two years earlier.

The team built two pipelines on one index with Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The **offline** side is a data-source sync on the `guidance-notes` S3 bucket: new PDFs are parsed, chunked and embedded, tracked by `doc_id` plus a content hash so a re-uploaded file never duplicates. The **online** side calls `RetrieveAndGenerate`, and the answer service checks every cited id against the `retrievedReferences` it actually received before showing anything.

It bit them in pilot week one. Someone rewrote the prompt template for a friendlier tone and deleted the `$output_format_instructions$` placeholder. Answers still read well, but citations came back empty and the id check rejected everything. Restoring the placeholder, plus a test that fails on empty citations, fixed it.

For the 300-page customs manual used by one small team, they skipped retrieval entirely: the whole manual sits in the **context window** with **prompt caching**. By the end of the pilot, typical lookups took under two minutes, and every answer pointed to a page.
inPractice.flow:
OFFLINE: S3 guidance-notes -> KB sync -> parse -> chunk -> embed -> index
ONLINE:  question -> RetrieveAndGenerate -> answer + citations
         -> cited ids in retrievedReferences?  yes -> show  no -> reject
customs manual (300 pages) -> whole text in context + prompt caching
inPractice.takeaway: I treat RAG as two pipelines sharing one index, verify every cited id in code, and skip retrieval entirely when the corpus fits in context with caching.

lesson.body:
RAG is two pipelines that share one index. The **offline** pipeline runs when documents arrive: parse (PDF text layer, OCR for scans, email headers), chunk, embed each chunk with an embedding model, and write `{chunk_id, doc_id, text, vector, metadata}` into an index. The **online** pipeline runs per question: embed the query with the *same* model, retrieve candidates (vector, lexical or both), optionally rerank, then build a prompt that contains the top chunks with their ids and ask the model to answer *and cite the ids*. Your answer service then checks that every cited id actually exists in the retrieved set before showing it, because models will invent plausible-looking citations.

Think of the offline side as a Kafka consumer that is idempotent on `doc_id` plus content hash, and the index as an Elasticsearch index with a `text` field and a `dense_vector` field side by side. Bedrock Knowledge Bases packages the same stages: a data-source sync does ingest, chunk and embed; `Retrieve` returns chunks (five by default); `RetrieveAndGenerate` adds generation and returns `citations` with `retrievedReferences`. Its prompt template must keep the `$output_format_instructions$` placeholder or citations disappear.

Most quality bugs live in retrieval, not generation. Anthropic's contextual retrieval experiment makes the point: prepending a one-sentence LLM-written context to each chunk before embedding cut top-20 retrieval failures by 35%, adding contextual BM25 took that to 49%, and reranking took it to 67%, for roughly $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching. And when the whole corpus is under about 200k tokens (roughly 500 pages), skip RAG entirely: put it in the context window with caching and move on.
lesson.snippet:
OFFLINE (per document)              ONLINE (per question)
S3 drop -> parse / OCR              question -> embed(query)
        -> chunk (structure-aware)           -> BM25 || kNN   [filter: matter, acl]
        -> embed(chunk)                      -> RRF fuse -> rerank top 50 -> keep 8
        -> index {text, vector, meta}        -> prompt with [chunk ids] -> LLM
                                             -> verify cited ids -> answer + citations

Failure map:
  wrong chunk ranked 40th ........ retrieval   (fix chunking / hybrid / rerank)
  clause split across chunks ..... chunking    (fix structure-aware splitting)
  right chunk present, ignored ... generation  (fix prompt / model / grounding check)
  doc never indexed .............. ingestion   (fix parser / idempotency / sync)

source.title: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases - How it works

cards.prompt: Which of these steps runs in the online (per-question) path of a RAG system rather than at ingestion time?
options: Building the HNSW graph over document vectors
Embedding the user's question
Splitting PDFs into chunks
OCR of scanned exhibits
cards.why: The query must be embedded at request time with the same model used for the chunks, so it lands in the same vector space. Graph building, chunking and OCR are all ingestion work; doing them per request would be unaffordable.

cards.prompt: In Anthropic's contextual retrieval experiment, contextual embeddings combined with contextual BM25 reduced the top-20 retrieval failure rate by roughly:
cards.why: 35% was contextual embeddings alone, 49% was embeddings plus contextual BM25 (5.7% to 2.9% failure rate), and 67% required adding a reranker. Candidates often quote the 67% headline for the wrong configuration.

cards.prompt: RAG is always the cheaper option compared with putting the whole document set into the prompt.
cards.why: Below roughly 200k tokens (about 500 pages) the entire corpus fits in context, and prompt caching makes repeated calls cheap and fast. A retrieval pipeline adds moving parts and a whole class of recall bugs for no benefit at that size.

cards.prompt: In Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the ___ placeholder must stay in the generation prompt template or the response will carry no citations.
cards.why: That placeholder injects model-specific formatting and citation instructions. Teams who customise the template and delete it lose citations silently, then blame the model.

cards.prompt: Why must the user's question be embedded with exactly the same embedding model (and version) as the indexed chunks?
options: Because newer models produce more dimensions and the index would overflow
Because vectors from different models occupy unrelated spaces, so distances between them are meaningless
Because the tokenizer would otherwise truncate the question
Because embedding APIs are billed per model and mixing models double-bills
cards.why: Similarity only means something between vectors produced by the same model. A dimension mismatch would at least fail loudly; a different model with the same dimension count fails silently with confident nonsense.

cards.prompt: If a model's answer cites a document id that is well formed, you can show it to the lawyer without further checks.
cards.why: Models fabricate plausible ids. The answer service must verify every cited id against the set of chunks actually placed in the prompt and drop or flag anything else; a fabricated citation in a legal memo is worse than no citation.

cards.prompt: With prompt caching, Anthropic estimated the one-time cost of generating contextual chunk descriptions at about $___ per million document tokens.
cards.why: The whole document is cached and each chunk is a short request against it, which is why the cost is near one dollar per million tokens rather than tens of dollars. That number makes contextual retrieval affordable for a 2-million-document corpus.

cards.prompt: Which of these is a generation-stage failure rather than a retrieval-stage failure?
options: The correct chunk was ranked 40th and cut off at k=10
The clause was split across two chunks so neither matched the question
The correct chunk was in the prompt but the model answered from its training data instead
A metadata filter on matter_id excluded the correct document
cards.why: Only the third case has the right evidence in front of the model; fixing it means prompting, model choice or a grounding check. The others are fixed in chunking, search or filtering, which is why evaluation must separate the two stages.

explain.prompt: Walk me through what happens between a lawyer typing a question and seeing an answer with citations.
explain.modelAnswer: Two things have already happened before the question: documents were parsed, chunked along their structure, embedded, and written to an index that holds the text, the vector and metadata like matter id and privilege flag. When the question arrives, I first resolve the user's entitlements into a filter. I embed the question with the same model used at ingest and run a hybrid query: BM25 for exact terms like section numbers, kNN for paraphrase, both pre-filtered by that entitlement filter, fused with reciprocal rank fusion. The top 50 or so go through a cross-encoder reranker and I keep the best eight. Those chunks go into the prompt with their ids, and the model is told to answer only from them and cite ids. Before I render, I verify every cited id is one I actually sent, attach the page and section from metadata, and log the whole trace: query, filter, chunk ids, tokens, latency. If nothing relevant survived the reranker, I say so rather than let the model improvise.
rubric: Separates offline ingestion from the online query path
Query embedded with the same model as the chunks
Permission filter derived server-side and applied at retrieval
Hybrid retrieval plus reranking before generation
Citations verified against retrieved chunk ids
Mentions tracing or an explicit 'not found' path

explain.prompt: When is RAG the wrong tool? Tell me when you would not build it.
explain.modelAnswer: RAG earns its complexity when the corpus is large, changes often, or has per-user access rules. If none of those hold, I would not build it. First, size: under roughly 200k tokens, about 500 pages, the whole set fits in the context window, and with prompt caching the repeated cost is small. A single matter's key contracts often fit, and stuffing them in gives better cross-document reasoning than retrieval does, with no recall risk. Second, when the question is not really about retrieval: summarising one document, drafting from a template, or structured extraction from a known file needs the file, not a search. Third, when answers must be exact and the source is a database: an ERP question like 'what is this employee's leave balance' should be a tool call to SQL, not similarity search over exported PDFs. Fourth, when nobody can label a golden set, because I cannot tell whether the retriever works. I would say this to a partner as: start with the simplest thing that answers the question correctly, measure, and add retrieval when the documents outgrow the window.
rubric: Context-window threshold around 200k tokens with prompt caching
Structured data belongs in tool calls, not vector search
Single-document tasks do not need retrieval
Cannot evaluate without a golden set, so start simple
Frames the decision in terms the client understands

scenarios.situation: A litigation partner wants a demo in three days: ask questions over one matter's 180-page set of agreements and correspondence. Your team proposes standing up a vector store, chunking pipeline and reranker on AWS before the demo. The firm has an AWS account and Bedrock access already.
scenarios.question: What do you propose?

options.text: Load the whole 180-page set into the model's context with prompt caching, ask the model to cite page numbers, and demo that; plan the retrieval pipeline for the full corpus afterwards.
options.why: 180 pages is well under the ~200k token point where RAG starts to pay off. You remove retrieval recall risk from the demo, deliver in a day, and learn which questions the partner actually asks before you design chunking.

options.text: Build the full pipeline in three days using Bedrock Knowledge Bases with default chunking so the demo already resembles production.
options.why: Knowledge Bases is fast to stand up and the demo would work, but default 300-token chunks on legal text will produce a few embarrassing mis-citations in front of a partner, and you are spending the three days on infrastructure instead of on the questions.

options.text: Fine-tune a model on the matter's documents so it knows the case without retrieval.
options.why: Fine-tuning does not reliably memorise facts, cannot cite sources, cannot be updated when a new document arrives, and takes longer than three days. It also spreads client-confidential text into model weights.

nodes.title: Chunking Strategies
nodes.tease: A 300-token window cut a contract clause in half. The model confidently cited the wrong party.

primer.problem: Search by meaning works on short passages, so every contract must be cut into pieces before it is indexed. Cut in the wrong place and a liability clause lands in one piece while its exception lands in the next, so the lawyer is handed half a rule as if it were the whole rule.
primer.picture: Picture splitting C# code for review. Cut every 300 lines and a method's signature lands in one file and its body in another; cut at class and method boundaries and each piece makes sense alone. Chunking is that choice for documents; each piece is a **chunk**. **Fixed-size** cuts by length, **semantic** cuts where the topic shifts, **hierarchical** searches small pieces but hands the model their larger parent, and **structure-aware** cuts at Article and Section headings and stamps each piece with its location, like `MSA > Art. 12 > 12.3`.

terms.def: The list of numbers a model produces for one chunk's text, so chunks with similar meaning get similar numbers.
The word-piece unit models count text in; roughly three quarters of an English word on average.
Text repeated at the end of one chunk and the start of the next, so a sentence near a cut is not lost.
Small child chunks are searched for precise matches, then each hit is swapped for the larger parent section that contains it.
A short path such as `MSA > Art. 12 > 12.3` written into the chunk text so it carries its location.
A capitalised word like 'Fees' whose meaning a contract fixes once, usually in Article 1, and then uses everywhere.
AWS's managed service that chunks, embeds and indexes documents from S3 and offers several built-in chunking strategies.

inPractice.setting: A legal-tech vendor indexing 40,000 MSAs for the contract teams of 30 law firms
inPractice.story:
The vendor's first index used Bedrock's default **fixed-size** chunking, about 300 tokens per chunk. Demos looked fine until an associate asked whether a supplier's indemnity covered negligence. The top chunk said 'the Supplier shall indemnify the Customer...', while the carve-out 'except where caused by Customer's negligence' sat in the next chunk, ranked 31st. The answer was confidently wrong.

They set the knowledge base to no chunking and moved splitting into a custom transformation Lambda, where their own parser walks Article, Section and sub-clause (a)(i). Each chunk now starts with a **breadcrumb** such as `MSA v3 > Art. 12 Liability > 12.3(b)` and carries section, page and defined-term metadata. Small child chunks are searched, then swapped for their parent section, so a clause arrives with the exception that modifies it.

The trade-off surfaced in the UI. The answer panel promised five sources, but **parent/child** collapse turned two hits from one section into a single parent, so lawyers sometimes saw three. The team stopped promising a count and raised `numberOfResults` to leave headroom.

They built the new index beside the old one and ran both on a 100-question golden set before switching the alias. Missed exceptions on liability questions fell from roughly one in four to one in twenty-five.
inPractice.flow:
S3 MSA PDFs -> KB sync (chunking: none) -> transformation Lambda
   -> split at Article / Section / (a)(i)
   -> child chunk '[MSA v3 > Art. 12 > 12.3(b)] ...' + parent_id
   -> embed children -> index
query -> match children -> swap for parent sections -> prompt
inPractice.takeaway: I chunk legal text along its own structure, with breadcrumbs and parent/child retrieval, so an obligation is never returned without the exception that modifies it.

lesson.body:
Chunking decides what a vector can ever mean. **Fixed-size** splits on a token budget with an overlap percentage; Bedrock's default is about 300 tokens, respecting sentence boundaries. It is cheap and predictable, and it happily puts 'the Supplier shall indemnify the Customer...' in one chunk and the carve-out 'except where caused by Customer's negligence' in the next, so the retriever returns an obligation without its exception.

**Hierarchical** (parent/child) chunking embeds small child chunks for precise matching, then at retrieval replaces each hit with its larger parent so the model sees surrounding context. In Bedrock you set parent and child max tokens plus an *absolute* overlap token count, and because children collapse into parents you can get fewer results than `numberOfResults`. AWS advises against it on S3 Vectors when combined sizes pass about 8,000 tokens, because of per-vector metadata limits.

**Semantic** chunking embeds each sentence with a buffer of neighbours and breaks where dissimilarity crosses a breakpoint percentile threshold. Boundaries follow topic shifts, but it costs foundation-model calls at ingest.

**Structure-aware** chunking uses the document's own skeleton. Legal text is a tree: Article, Section, sub-clause (a)(i), a Definitions section whose capitalised terms are referenced everywhere, schedules and exhibits, email threads with headers. Split at those boundaries, prepend a breadcrumb such as `MSA v3 > Art. 12 Liability > 12.3(b)` to the chunk text, and store section, page and defined-term metadata. Lawyers then get the clause they asked about together with the one it modifies, and citations that point to a page. Bedrock attaches full-page or full-table context to chunks from parsed markdown when that context is 10,000 characters or less; for anything beyond that, choose no chunking and split in a custom transformation Lambda, where your own parser knows what a clause is.
lesson.snippet:
import re
HEADING = re.compile(r'^(ARTICLE|Article|Section|SCHEDULE)\s+[\dIVX]+[.\d()a-z]*', re.M)

def chunk_legal(doc_id: str, text: str, max_tokens: int = 400):
    bounds = [m.start() for m in HEADING.finditer(text)] + [len(text)]
    crumbs: list[str] = []
    for start, end in zip(bounds, bounds[1:]):
        section = text[start:end].strip()
        heading = section.splitlines()[0]
        depth = heading.count('.') + 1          # 12 -> 1, 12.3 -> 2
        crumbs = crumbs[:depth - 1] + [heading]
        breadcrumb = ' > '.join(crumbs)
        for piece in split_on_sentences(section, max_tokens):
            yield {
                'doc_id': doc_id,
                'section': heading,
                'text': f'[{breadcrumb}]\n{piece}',   # breadcrumb is embedded too
                'parent_id': f'{doc_id}#{crumbs[0]}',  # for small-to-big retrieval
            }

source.title: How content chunking works for knowledge bases - Amazon Bedrock

cards.prompt: What does Bedrock Knowledge Bases' default chunking do?
options: Treats each document as one chunk
Splits into chunks of about 300 tokens while preserving sentence boundaries
Splits at semantic breakpoints using an embedding model
Splits into 512-token chunks with 20% overlap
cards.why: Default chunking is roughly 300 tokens, sentence-aware, with no configurable overlap. 512 tokens with overlap is what you would configure under fixed-size chunking, and semantic splitting is a separate, paid option.

cards.prompt: With hierarchical chunking in Bedrock, what does the retriever return to the model?
options: The matching child chunk only, to keep the prompt short
Both the child and all its siblings
The parent chunk that contains the matching child, which can make the result count smaller than requested
A summary of the parent generated at ingest
cards.why: Small children give precise matching; the parent gives the model context. Because several children can map to one parent, the returned count may be lower than numberOfResults, which surprises teams who size k by the child count.

cards.prompt: In Bedrock hierarchical chunking, overlap between chunks is expressed as a percentage, just like fixed-size chunking.
cards.why: Hierarchical overlap is an absolute number of tokens applied between consecutive parents and consecutive children. Fixed-size chunking is the one that takes an overlap percentage.

cards.prompt: Bedrock semantic chunking places a boundary where the sentence-to-sentence dissimilarity exceeds the ___ percentile threshold.
cards.why: The breakpoint percentile threshold, together with buffer size and max tokens, are the three semantic-chunking knobs. A higher threshold means fewer, larger chunks.

cards.prompt: Why do contracts specifically punish naive fixed-size chunking?
options: Contracts are too long for any embedding model
Clauses modify each other through cross-references and defined terms, so a chunk without its heading, exception or definition is misleading
Legal English uses rare words that embedding models cannot represent
PDF contracts cannot be parsed into text
cards.why: 'Subject to Section 4.2' and capitalised Defined Terms make meaning non-local. Structure-aware chunks carry the heading breadcrumb and link to parents and definitions, which fixed windows cannot do. Rare vocabulary is a problem for BM25 and embeddings alike but not the main failure.

cards.prompt: Bedrock attaches full-page or full-table context to a chunk from parsed content only when that context is at most:
options: 1,000 characters
10,000 characters
100,000 characters
There is no limit
cards.why: Above 10,000 characters the matched chunk is returned as is. The limit exists because the context is stored as vector metadata, which has its own size caps, especially on S3 Vectors.

cards.prompt: Semantic chunking in Bedrock is free, because it is just a different text splitter.
cards.why: Semantic chunking embeds sentence windows with a foundation model to find boundaries, so AWS bills the model usage on top of ingestion. For a 2-million-document corpus that is a line item worth estimating.

cards.prompt: Choosing ___ chunking in Bedrock treats each file as a single chunk and removes page numbers from citations.
cards.why: No chunking is the escape hatch for pre-split documents or a custom Lambda transformer, but you lose the x-amz-bedrock-kb-document-page-number metadata, so citations can no longer point to a page.

explain.prompt: Why do legal documents need structure-aware chunking? Give me the mechanism and one concrete failure.
explain.modelAnswer: An embedding represents one chunk, so the chunk boundary decides what a vector can mean. Legal documents have non-local meaning: Section 12.3 is 'subject to Section 4.2', Defined Terms are set once in Article 1 and used everywhere, and exceptions sit in the sentence after the obligation. A fixed 300-token window ignores that structure. Concrete failure: a liability cap clause reads 'The Supplier's aggregate liability shall not exceed the Fees paid in the preceding twelve months', and the next sentence says 'This limitation shall not apply to breaches of Section 9 (Confidentiality) or to indemnities under Section 11.' The window ends between them. A lawyer asks whether the cap applies to a confidentiality breach, retrieval returns the first sentence, and the model confidently answers yes, with a citation. Structure-aware chunking splits at Article and Section boundaries, prepends a breadcrumb like 'MSA > Art. 12 Limitation of Liability > 12.3' into the embedded text, stores section and page as metadata, and keeps a parent reference so the model sees the whole clause. The breadcrumb also helps BM25 because the section number is now literally in the chunk.
rubric: Vector meaning is bounded by the chunk boundary
Cross-references and defined terms make legal meaning non-local
A concrete clause-split failure with a wrong answer
Breadcrumb heading embedded into the chunk text
Parent/child or metadata for section and page
Benefit for citations or lexical search

scenarios.situation: A firm has indexed 40,000 master service agreements with fixed 300-token chunks. Associates report that answers about liability caps cite the right agreement but the wrong clause, and exceptions are routinely missed. The index took four days and $3,000 in embedding costs to build. Go-live is in three weeks.
scenarios.question: What change do you make?

options.text: Re-chunk along Article/Section structure with heading breadcrumbs and parent/child retrieval, rebuild into a new index alongside the old one, and compare both on a 100-question golden set before switching the alias.
options.why: The failure is a chunk-boundary problem, so only a chunking change fixes it. Rebuilding is a known $3,000 and four days, well inside three weeks, and the golden-set comparison turns the change from a hope into a measurement.

options.text: Raise the fixed chunk size to 1,500 tokens so whole clauses usually fit, and rebuild.
options.why: Bigger windows catch more exceptions and cost the same rebuild, but they dilute the vector, make precision worse, and still cut clauses at arbitrary points. It is a patch, not a fix.

options.text: Keep the index and raise numberOfResults to 50 so the missing exception is probably somewhere in the prompt.
options.why: Fifty chunks per question multiplies token cost, pushes the relevant text into the middle of a long prompt where models attend poorly, and still returns clauses without their headings. You pay more for the same wrong citations.

nodes.title: Hybrid Search and RRF
nodes.tease: Your vector index can't find 'Section 12.3(b)'. Your old BM25 index can. Why not use both?

primer.problem: Lawyers search in two ways. Sometimes they type an exact identifier like a Bates number or 'Section 12.3(b)'; sometimes they describe an idea in their own words, like 'can we walk away without penalty'. Keyword search nails the first and misses the second, meaning-based search does the opposite, so you need both merged into one list.
primer.picture: You already know half: Elasticsearch BM25 matches words. Add a second query on a `dense_vector` field that finds passages close in meaning even with no shared words. Now you have two ranked lists whose scores are in different units, like adding kilometres to kilograms. **Reciprocal rank fusion** ignores scores and uses positions only: each passage earns `1/(60 + rank)` from every list it appears in, and the totals set the final order. OpenSearch, the open-source Elasticsearch fork that AWS started, offers the same idea.
primer.sketch:
question --+--> BM25 query  --> list A: #1 doc7, #2 doc3, ...
           +--> kNN query   --> list B: #1 doc3, #2 doc9, ...
                                   |
            RRF: score = sum of 1/(60 + rank) per list
                                   v
                    fused list: doc3, doc7, doc9, ...

terms.def: Elasticsearch's default keyword-scoring formula; its scores have no fixed upper limit and depend on the whole collection.
A list of numbers a model produces for a text so that texts with similar meaning sit close together.
Finding the k stored vectors nearest the query's vector, usually through an approximate graph index called HNSW.
A closeness score between two vectors that always falls between -1 and 1, with 1 meaning same direction.
The alternative to RRF: rescale each list's scores to a common range such as 0 to 1, then combine them with tuned weights.
A unique identifier like PRIV-0002931 stamped on every page produced in litigation, so each page can be referenced exactly.
A score from 0 to 1 for how well the top ten results put the most relevant documents first.

inPractice.setting: A DIY and hardware e-shop answering questions over 600,000 SKUs and their manuals
inPractice.story:
The retailer's support assistant answered questions from product manuals. It started with pure vector search, which handled paraphrase well: 'something to stop the door slamming' found soft-close hinges. It was useless on part numbers. A customer typing `HX-4410-B` got four similar-sounding hinges and not the one they owned.

The team already ran Elasticsearch for the storefront, so they added a `dense_vector` field beside `text` and wrapped a `standard` BM25 retriever and a `knn` retriever in an `rrf` retriever. An earlier prototype had simply added BM25 score to cosine similarity; BM25 ran into the twenties while cosine stayed below 1, so the vector side barely counted. **Reciprocal rank fusion** fixed that by ignoring scores and summing `1/(60 + rank)` across lists.

The bite came from `rank_window_size`. It sat at the default of 10 with `size: 10`, so a manual chunk ranked 14th by BM25 and 3rd by kNN only earned its kNN share and lost to chunks found by both. Widening the window to 50 lifted recall on their test queries for a modest CPU cost.

They kept `rank_constant` at 60. Once they had a few thousand judged queries they trialled weighted **score normalization** as the tuned alternative, but kept RRF as the default because it needed no recalibration when the catalogue changed.
inPractice.flow:
query 'HX-4410-B hinge stiff'
  |-> standard (BM25 on text)  -> ranked list A
  |-> knn (vector, k=50)       -> ranked list B
  rrf: rank_constant 60, rank_window_size 50
  -> fused top 10 -> prompt -> answer citing manual page
inPractice.takeaway: BM25 and vectors fail differently, so I fuse them with reciprocal rank fusion, which uses ranks instead of scores, and size the rank window to protect recall.

lesson.body:
Lexical and dense retrieval fail differently. BM25 is unbeatable on exact tokens: Bates numbers like `PRIV-0002931`, case numbers, defined terms, 'Section 12.3(b)'. Dense vectors win when the lawyer paraphrases: 'can we walk away without penalty' should find 'termination for convenience'. Hybrid search runs both and merges.

You cannot add the scores. BM25 is unbounded and corpus-dependent; cosine lives in [-1, 1]. **Reciprocal rank fusion** sidesteps scale entirely: each document scores `sum(1 / (k + rank_i))` over the result lists it appears in, with `k = 60` from Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (2009). A document ranked 1st in one list and 3rd in the other gets 1/61 + 1/63; a document that appears in only one list needs a very high rank to compete. No tuning, no calibration.

In Elasticsearch this is the `rrf` retriever wrapping child retrievers, typically a `standard` (BM25) retriever and a `knn` retriever. `rank_constant` defaults to 60 and `rank_window_size` to 10; the window must be at least `size`, and widening it to 50 or 100 improves recall at some CPU cost. Retrievers and RRF went GA together in 8.16, for Enterprise-licensed clusters. A `filter` inside the `knn` clause is applied as a pre-filter during HNSW traversal, so you still get k matching documents. OpenSearch offers the `hybrid` query with a search pipeline: the `normalization-processor` (min_max or l2 normalization; arithmetic, geometric or harmonic mean; per-clause weights) or, since 2.19, the `score-ranker-processor` with `technique: rrf`. OpenSearch's own BEIR benchmark found RRF about 3.86% lower NDCG@10 than a tuned score-normalization pipeline, which is the trade: RRF is the robust default, weighted normalization is what you tune once you have relevance judgments.

Your Elasticsearch background is the edge here. Analyzers, synonyms for legal abbreviations, `match_phrase` for quoted clauses, and `semantic_text` with ELSER as a third sparse signal all still matter inside a RAG system.

cards.prompt: How does reciprocal rank fusion score a document that appears in several ranked lists?
options: Average of its normalized scores across lists
Sum over lists of 1 / (k + rank), with k typically 60
Its best single rank across lists
Product of its BM25 score and cosine similarity
cards.why: RRF uses only ranks, so BM25 and cosine never need to be made comparable. Averaging normalized scores is the alternative (OpenSearch normalization-processor) and needs min/max or l2 normalization plus weights to tune.

cards.prompt: Elasticsearch's rrf retriever has a rank_constant parameter that defaults to ___.
cards.why: k=60 comes from the original 2009 paper and is the default in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Larger k flattens the curve so lower-ranked documents matter more; smaller k makes top ranks dominate.

cards.prompt: Why can't you simply add a BM25 score and a cosine similarity to rank hybrid results?
options: Elasticsearch forbids combining them in one query
BM25 is unbounded and depends on corpus statistics while cosine is bounded in [-1, 1], so one signal swamps the other
Cosine similarity is always negative for text
BM25 scores are integers and cannot be summed with floats
cards.why: A BM25 score of 27.4 added to a cosine of 0.81 is just BM25 with noise. You either normalize both (and tune weights) or fuse on ranks with RRF.

cards.prompt: In an Elasticsearch rrf retriever, rank_window_size must be at least as large as the request's size.
cards.why: Each child retriever contributes rank_window_size results to fusion, and the fused list is then trimmed to size; a window smaller than size would make the request incoherent. The default window is 10, which is usually too small for hybrid recall.

cards.prompt: In OpenSearch, which search-pipeline processor implements reciprocal rank fusion for a hybrid query?
options: normalization-processor
score-ranker-processor
rrf-processor
hybrid-fusion-processor
cards.why: score-ranker-processor (added in 2.19) fuses by rank with technique rrf. normalization-processor is the score-based path with min_max/l2 and weighted means; the other two names do not exist and are rejected as invalid processor types.

cards.prompt: Which query is BM25 most likely to win outright against a dense retriever?
options: 'what are our options if the supplier keeps missing deadlines'
'documents mentioning PRIV-0002931'
'is there anything about leaving the contract early'
'who is responsible when a subcontractor messes up'
cards.why: A Bates number is a rare exact token; embeddings tokenize it into fragments and lose it, while BM25 matches it precisely. The others are paraphrases where dense retrieval shines, which is the whole case for hybrid.

cards.prompt: In OpenSearch's published BEIR benchmarks, RRF outperformed tuned score normalization on NDCG@10.
cards.why: RRF averaged about 3.86% lower NDCG@10 than the tuned normalization pipeline, with comparable latency. RRF wins on robustness and zero tuning; once you have relevance judgments, weighted normalization can edge it.

cards.prompt: In Elasticsearch, a filter placed inside the knn clause is applied as a ___-filter during the HNSW search, so k matching documents are still returned.
cards.why: A pre-filter restricts the graph traversal to allowed documents. A post_filter runs after the top-k is chosen and can leave you with far fewer than k results, which matters when the filter is a strict permission boundary.

explain.prompt: Explain hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion to me as if I had only ever used Elasticsearch for keyword search.
explain.modelAnswer: You already have half of it. BM25 scores documents on term matches, so it is excellent at exact things: Bates numbers, clause numbers, defined terms. What it cannot do is understand that 'leave the contract early' means 'termination for convenience'. Vector search fixes that: an embedding model turns both the question and each chunk into a vector, and kNN on a dense_vector field finds chunks whose meaning is close even when no words overlap. Hybrid search runs both queries and merges the results. The catch is that a BM25 score of 27 and a cosine of 0.8 cannot be added. Reciprocal rank fusion ignores scores and uses ranks: each document gets the sum over the lists of 1 divided by 60 plus its rank. Something ranked first in both lists scores about 0.033; something ranked first in one and absent from the other scores about 0.016. In Elasticsearch this is the rrf retriever with a standard child and a knn child; rank_constant defaults to 60 and I would raise rank_window_size from 10 to 50. Your analyzers, synonyms and filters still apply, so nothing you know is wasted.

Why raw scores cannot be summed

Mentions rank_window_size or filters still applying

explain.prompt: When would you choose weighted score normalization over RRF, and what would you need first?
explain.modelAnswer: RRF is my default because it needs no tuning and is robust to a bad sub-retriever: a document only ranks high if it ranks high somewhere. But it throws away score magnitude. If BM25 is extremely confident, say an exact Bates number match with a score ten times the runner-up, RRF treats it as just 'rank one', the same as a marginal first place. Weighted normalization keeps that gap: min-max or l2 normalize each list, then combine with weights, for example 0.7 lexical and 0.3 semantic for an identifier-heavy eDiscovery workload. OpenSearch's own benchmarks show a tuned normalization pipeline beating RRF by a few percent of NDCG@10. The precondition is relevance judgments: a golden set of queries with labelled relevant chunks so I can actually measure NDCG and pick weights, and ideally per-query-type routing, because the right weights for identifier lookups differ from those for conceptual questions. Without judgments, tuning weights is guessing, and RRF's zero-tuning behaviour is the safer production choice. So: ship RRF, build the golden set, then test normalization as an A/B.

Normalization needs weights, and weights need relevance judgments
Mentions min_max/l2 and weighted combination
Cites the benchmark direction (tuned normalization slightly ahead)
Recommends RRF first, measure, then tune

scenarios.situation: An eDiscovery review team's new semantic search over 1.2 million emails misses exact Bates numbers and defined terms, which paralegals search for constantly. The firm already runs an OpenSearch cluster for its legacy keyword review tool. The vendor who built the vector search proposes fine-tuning the embedding model on legal data.
scenarios.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: Add a hybrid query with a BM25 clause and a kNN clause fused by RRF in the existing OpenSearch cluster, and verify on a set of paralegal queries that identifiers now hit.
options.why: Exact identifiers are a lexical problem and BM25 solves it immediately; the cluster and the review team's expectations already exist. RRF needs no tuning and the fix can ship in days with a measurable before/after.

options.text: Fine-tune the embedding model on the firm's legal corpus so it represents Bates numbers and defined terms better.
options.why: Domain fine-tuning can lift semantic recall, but embeddings fundamentally blur rare identifiers, the training data is privileged, and it forces a full re-embed of 1.2 million emails. It is a later optimisation, not the fix for exact-match misses.

options.text: Raise k from 10 to 200 on the vector query so the exact matches are more likely to appear somewhere in the results.
options.why: A Bates number the embedding never represented will not surface at k=200 either, and reviewers now wade through 200 results. It raises cost and latency without addressing the cause.

nodes.title: Rerankers and Permission Filters
nodes.tease: The reranker scored it 0.97. The associate wasn't cleared to see it. Which check runs first?

primer.problem: Two things go wrong at the top of search results. The best passage is often in the top 50 but not the top 5, so the model reads near-misses. Worse, a passage from a matter the lawyer is walled off from can surface, and once it reaches the model no instruction reliably keeps it out.
primer.picture: Two gates in a fixed order. First a **permission filter**, built on the server from who the user is, goes inside the search query itself, exactly like a C# authorization handler appending `WHERE matter_id IN (...)` or SQL Server row-level security: forbidden documents are never even looked at. Then, on the 50 or so permitted results, a **reranker** reads the question and each passage together and re-scores them, and you keep the best 5 to 10. Fast search finds candidates; a slow, careful reader picks the winners.
primer.sketch:
user identity -> entitlement service -> allowed matter ids
                                            |
question -> keyword + vector search, filter INSIDE ->  top 50 permitted
         -> reranker reads (question, passage) pairs -> keep top 8
         -> prompt -> model

terms.def: A model that embeds query and document separately, so document vectors can be computed ahead of time and searched fast.
A model that reads the question and one passage together and outputs a relevance score; accurate but too slow for millions.
A firm's rule that certain lawyers must not see a given matter's documents, usually because of a conflict of interest.
The system of record that says which matters and clients a given user is allowed to see.
A restriction applied during the search itself, so only permitted documents are considered and you still get k results.
A restriction applied after the top results are chosen; it can leave few or no results and is not a security boundary.
A lawyer-client communication protected from disclosure, flagged in metadata so search can exclude it.

inPractice.setting: A health insurer's case-management assistant for 900 nurses across six regions
inPractice.story:
Nurse case managers asked the assistant about care plans, discharge notes and prior authorisations, and each nurse may only see members in their own region. The first build retrieved the top 10 chunks from OpenSearch and then dropped any the nurse was not entitled to. In testing, a north-region nurse asked about a common diabetes protocol and got zero sources: all ten hits belonged to other regions, and they had already been read and logged.

The fix was the lesson's rule: the query is the gate. On every request the API asks the **entitlement service** for the nurse's permitted `region_id` and member ids and pushes them as a **pre-filter** inside both the BM25 and the kNN clause, deny by default. The index still used the deprecated `nmslib` engine, which post-filters, so they rebuilt it on `faiss`.

With 50 permitted candidates guaranteed, they added a **cross-encoder reranker**: the `Rerank` API with `cohere.rerank-v3-5:0`, because they run in us-east-1, where `amazon.rerank-v1:0` is not offered. Only the top 8 reach the prompt. Prompts shrank by more than half, and nurses stopped seeing near-miss protocols for the wrong condition.

A regression test now replays the original question as a north-region nurse and fails if any chunk from another region appears.
inPractice.flow:
nurse token -> entitlement service -> permitted region + member ids
question -> BM25 + kNN (faiss), pre-filter inside both -> top 50
         -> Rerank cohere.rerank-v3-5:0 -> keep 8
         -> prompt -> answer + sources
inPractice.takeaway: Permissions go into the retrieval query as a server-side pre-filter, never a post-filter or a prompt instruction; then a cross-encoder reranks the permitted top 50 down to eight.

lesson.body:
Retrieval is two stages because the cheap stage is wrong at the top. A bi-encoder scores query and document independently, so document vectors can be precomputed and searched in milliseconds, but the model never sees query and passage together. A **cross-encoder reranker** reads the pair `(query, passage)` jointly and emits a relevance score. It cannot be precomputed, so you run it on the top 50-100 candidates from hybrid search and keep the best 5-10 for the prompt. Fewer, better chunks means a shorter prompt and a cheaper, more faithful answer.

On AWS the `Rerank` API in `bedrock-agent-runtime` serves `cohere.rerank-v3-5:0` and `amazon.rerank-v1:0` (the Amazon model is not offered in us-east-1), and Knowledge Bases accepts a `rerankingConfiguration` on `Retrieve`. Elasticsearch has the `text_similarity_reranker` retriever, defaulting to the built-in `.rerank-v1-elasticsearch` endpoint with `rank_window_size` 10, and it can call Cohere or Vertex rerank endpoints instead.

**Metadata filters are the security boundary.** Every chunk carries `client_id`, `matter_id`, `custodian`, `doc_date` and privilege flags. The filter is derived server-side from the authenticated user's entitlements and pushed into the retrieval query, exactly as a C# authorization handler appends `WHERE tenant_id = @tenant` to every query, or as SQL Server row-level security does. In Elasticsearch, document level security turns a role query into a cached BitSet so kNN only traverses permitted documents, and a `filter` inside `knn` is a pre-filter. In OpenSearch, efficient filtering requires the lucene or faiss engine (nmslib post-filters and is deprecated), which is why Bedrock Knowledge Bases requires `faiss` for metadata filtering. Bedrock filters come from `<file>.<ext>.metadata.json` sidecars and use `equals`, `in`, `greaterThan` and friends, combined with `andAll`/`orAll`, up to five per group.

Post-filtering is a trap: retrieve k=10, then drop forbidden documents, and you return three results or none, having already looked at documents the user may not see. The model is never the gate; the query is.

cards.prompt: What makes a cross-encoder reranker more accurate than the first-stage vector search, and why can't it replace it?
options: It uses a larger embedding dimension; it is simply more expensive to store
It scores query and passage jointly in one forward pass, so it cannot be precomputed and must run only on a shortlist
It is trained on legal data; it needs a GPU
It uses BM25 internally; it cannot handle paraphrase
cards.why: Seeing the pair together lets the model weigh exactly how the passage answers the query, but that means one inference per (query, document) pair at request time. Bi-encoders precompute document vectors, which is why they handle the first stage over millions of chunks.

cards.prompt: Which reranker models does the Amazon Bedrock Rerank API support?
options: Cohere Rerank 3.5 and Amazon Rerank 1.0
Cohere Rerank 2 and Titan Rerank
Any Bedrock text model with a rerank prompt
Elastic Rerank and Cohere Rerank 3.5
cards.why: The two model IDs are cohere.rerank-v3-5:0 and amazon.rerank-v1:0. Elastic Rerank is Elasticsearch's built-in model, and using a general text model as a reranker is possible but far slower and more expensive per pair.

cards.prompt: Amazon Rerank 1.0 is available in US East (N. Virginia).
cards.why: AWS documents that only Cohere Rerank 3.5 is offered in us-east-1; Amazon Rerank 1.0 is in Oregon, Frankfurt, Tokyo and Canada (Central). For a European client, Frankfurt supports both.

cards.prompt: Elasticsearch's text_similarity_reranker retriever defaults its inference_id to ___.
cards.why: That is Elastic's built-in cross-encoder, so a reranking stage needs no external API. Point inference_id at a Cohere or Vertex endpoint if you want a different model.

cards.prompt: Where should 'this associate may not see Matter B' be enforced in a RAG system?
options: In the system prompt: instruct the model never to reveal documents from other matters
As a filter on matter_id derived from the authenticated identity and applied inside the retrieval query
By post-processing the answer and redacting mentions of Matter B
By asking the model to check permissions with a tool before answering
cards.why: Only a retrieval-time filter guarantees forbidden text never enters the prompt. Prompts can be jailbroken, redaction misses paraphrase, and a model-initiated permission check is optional by construction.

cards.prompt: You run kNN with k=10 and then remove documents the user cannot access. What is the most likely visible symptom?
options: Results are slower because the filter runs twice
You return far fewer than 10 results, sometimes none, even when permitted relevant documents exist
Duplicate documents appear in the results
The vector scores become negative
cards.why: Post-filtering discards hits after the top-k was already chosen. If most near neighbours belong to other matters, nothing survives. Pre-filtering inside the knn clause keeps traversing until k permitted documents are found.

cards.prompt: For Bedrock Knowledge Bases on OpenSearch Serverless, metadata filtering requires the vector index to use the faiss engine rather than nmslib.
cards.why: Efficient (pre-)filtering in OpenSearch is supported by the lucene and faiss engines; nmslib only post-filters and is deprecated. AWS tells you to recreate the index with faiss if you built it with nmslib.

cards.prompt: In an S3 data source for Bedrock Knowledge Bases, filterable attributes for contract.pdf live in a sidecar file named contract.pdf.___ .
cards.why: The <file>.<ext>.metadata.json convention is how matter_id, custodian, privilege and dates become filterable at query time. Forgetting the sidecar silently makes those documents unfilterable, which in a permission filter means they are excluded or exposed depending on your default.

explain.prompt: How do you make sure a lawyer never sees a document from a matter they are walled off from?
explain.modelAnswer: I treat it like row-level security, not like a prompt problem. Every chunk is indexed with matter_id, client_id, custodian and a privilege flag, so the data carries its own labels. At request time the API authenticates the user and asks an entitlement service which matters they may see; the ethical wall lives there, maintained by risk and compliance, not in my code. That list becomes a filter that I inject into the retrieval query server-side, inside the knn clause and the BM25 clause, so it is a pre-filter: the vector search never traverses forbidden documents and I still get k permitted results. Nothing from the request body can widen it. Deny by default: no entitlement, no results. The reranker and the model only ever see what survived the filter, so even a jailbreak cannot surface a walled-off document. Then I log the filter and the chunk ids on every request, so an auditor can prove what the user could and could not see. The model is never the gate, because a gate the model can skip is not a gate.
rubric: Permission attributes indexed on every chunk
Entitlements resolved server-side from the authenticated identity
Filter applied as a pre-filter inside the retrieval query
Deny by default, nothing client-supplied can widen the filter
Audit logging of filter and chunk ids
Explicitly rejects prompt instructions as the control

explain.prompt: Why add a reranker if hybrid search already works, and what does it cost you?
explain.modelAnswer: Hybrid search is good at recall: the right chunk is usually somewhere in the top 50. It is weaker at precision at the top, because the bi-encoder scored the question and the chunk separately and never read them together. A cross-encoder reranker reads each (question, chunk) pair jointly and re-scores the shortlist, so the eight chunks I put in the prompt are the eight that actually answer the question. That buys three things: better faithfulness, because the model is not distracted by near-misses; a shorter prompt, so lower generation cost; and clean citations, because the top chunk is the right clause. Anthropic's numbers show this: contextual hybrid retrieval cut failures by 49%, adding a reranker took it to 67%. The costs are per-query latency, in my experience tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds for a 50-pair shortlist depending on passage length and the hosted model, a per-request fee for a hosted model like Cohere Rerank 3.5 on Bedrock, and operational dependency on another endpoint. I keep the shortlist to 50-100 and skip reranking for identifier lookups where BM25 is already exact.
rubric: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder distinction
Reranker improves precision at the top of the list
Benefits: faithfulness, shorter prompt, better citations
Costs: latency, per-call fee, extra dependency
Shortlist size (50-100) and when to skip

scenarios.situation: A firm's conflicts team has erected an ethical wall: associates on Matter A must not see anything from Matter B, which involves the opposing party. Both matters are indexed in the same OpenSearch cluster. During testing, an associate on Matter A asks a broad question and the answer cites a Matter B email. The system prompt already says 'only use documents from the user's matters'.
scenarios.question: How do you fix it before go-live?

options.text: Resolve the user's permitted matter ids from the entitlement system on every request and apply them as a pre-filter inside both the kNN and BM25 clauses, deny by default, and add a test that replays the leaking question for a Matter A user.
options.why: The leak proves the prompt is not a control. A server-derived pre-filter means Matter B chunks never enter retrieval, the reranker, or the prompt, and the regression test keeps it that way.

options.text: Keep retrieval as is but drop any chunk whose matter_id is not permitted after retrieval and before the prompt is built.
options.why: This does stop the leak into the prompt, but it is post-filtering: results shrink unpredictably, forbidden documents are still fetched and scored, and a bug in that one function leaks everything. Push the filter into the query.

options.text: Strengthen the system prompt with explicit matter ids and add a line telling the model to refuse if it is unsure.
options.why: The forbidden text is already in the prompt at that point; one injection or one model slip and it is on screen. A regulator will not accept 'we asked the model nicely' as an ethical wall.

nodes.title: Embedding Models
nodes.tease: You upgraded the embedding model on Friday. By Monday half of search returned garbage. What broke?

primer.problem: Search by meaning needs every passage turned into numbers a computer can compare. At millions of passages those numbers cost serious memory, and they only make sense next to numbers from the same model, so a quiet model upgrade can make search return confident garbage without a single error.
primer.picture: Think of an embedding model as a function `float[] Embed(string text)` that always returns an array of the same length, built so texts with similar meaning get nearby arrays. Each model has its own coordinate system, like two maps with different origins: a point from model A means nothing on model B's map, even if both arrays have 1,024 numbers. You store the arrays in an Elasticsearch `dense_vector` field, and you treat a model change like a mapping change: new index, test it, flip the alias.

terms.def: The fixed-length array of numbers a model produces for a piece of text, positioned so similar meanings sit close together.
How many numbers each embedding holds, such as 1,024; more dimensions cost more memory per stored vector.
Storing each vector's numbers in fewer bits, such as 1 byte or even 1 bit instead of 4 bytes, trading a little accuracy for memory.
A graph index that links each vector to its near neighbours so nearest-match search skips most of the collection.
The word-piece unit models read and count text in; input limits like 8,192 tokens are measured in these.
Building a complete new index beside the live one, testing it, then switching traffic over in one step.
A fixed list of real questions with known correct passages and answers, used to measure search quality before and after changes.

inPractice.setting: A national news publisher's archive assistant over 3 million articles since 1990
inPractice.story:
Reporters used the assistant to ask the archive things like what a minister had said about rail fares before an election. Articles were chunked and embedded with Titan Text Embeddings V2 at 1,024 dimensions into an Elasticsearch `dense_vector` field: about 15 million chunks, roughly 60 GB of raw float32 vectors before the HNSW graph.

Trouble started when a developer switched the ingest job to Cohere Embed v4 for new articles only, set to 1,024 dimensions so the mapping still accepted it. No errors, no alerts. A week later reporters noticed that questions about recent stories returned confident, irrelevant 1990s pieces. Queries were embedded with one model and part of the index with another, and those **embedding spaces** are unrelated even when both arrays hold 1,024 numbers.

They rolled ingest back, then did the change properly as a **blue/green reindex**. A new `archive-v2` index got an `embed_model` keyword on every chunk, `bbq_hnsw` **quantization**, and 512 dimensions, after the golden set showed recall@10 within a point of 1,024. Queries for v2 were embedded with Embed v4 only, both indexes ran the 150-question golden set, and one alias flip moved traffic.

The new index needed a fraction of the memory, and v1 stayed a week for instant rollback. Ingest now refuses any chunk whose `embed_model` differs from its index's.
inPractice.flow:
ingest -> chunk -> embed (one model per index) -> archive-v1 | archive-v2
query  -> embed with the SAME model as the target index
golden set (150 q) -> recall@10 on v1 and v2
POST _aliases: archive -> v2   (v1 kept a week for rollback)
inPractice.takeaway: Vectors only compare within one model and version, so I treat an embedding change like a mapping change: new index, golden-set comparison, then an alias flip.

lesson.body:
An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector so that nearby vectors mean similar things. Query and documents must be embedded by the same model and version; vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces, so a mixed index returns confident nonsense. That one fact drives most of the operations.

Know the shapes. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 (`amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0`) takes up to 8,192 tokens or 50,000 characters and outputs 1,024 dimensions by default, with 512 and 256 available; AWS reports about 99% of retrieval accuracy retained at 512 and 97% at 256. Cohere Embed v4 defaults to 1,536 dimensions (256/512/1024/1536 selectable), accepts 128k tokens, and embeds images and PDFs as well as text. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large is 3,072 dimensions. Inputs longer than the limit get truncated or rejected depending on the SDK, so chunk before you embed.

Dimensions cost memory. One float32 1,024-dim vector is 4 KB; 2 million documents at five chunks each is 10 million vectors, about 40 GB raw before the HNSW graph. Quantization is how production survives: Elasticsearch has indexed float vectors as `int8_hnsw` by default since 8.14 (4x smaller), switched the default to `bbq_hnsw` for 384+ dimensions in 9.1 (around 32x), and added `bbq_disk` in 9.2, which becomes the default under an Enterprise licence in 9.4. HNSW defaults are `m: 16` and `ef_construction: 100`, and a `dense_vector` field caps at 4,096 dimensions.

Re-embed when the model, its version or the chunking changes, never because one document changed; a changed document re-embeds only its own chunks. Treat a model change as a blue/green reindex: build the new index alongside the old one, embed queries with the new model only against the new index, run the golden set on both, then flip an alias, the same way you would roll an Elasticsearch mapping change.

2,048 tokens

cards.prompt: A deploy switched the query embedding to a new model while the index still holds vectors from the old one. Both are 1,024 dimensions. What happens?
options: Nothing; same dimensions means compatible vectors
Elasticsearch rejects the query with a dimension error
Queries run without error but return semantically unrelated chunks
