cards.prompt: Reducing Titan V2 output from 1,024 to 512 dimensions loses roughly half of its retrieval accuracy.
cards.why: AWS reports about 99% of retrieval accuracy retained at 512 and about 97% at 256, while halving or quartering vector storage. Dimension reduction is one of the cheapest cost levers you have.

cards.prompt: An Elasticsearch dense_vector field can have at most ___ dimensions.
cards.why: 4,096 is the hard cap, comfortably above text-embedding-3-large's 3,072. If dims is omitted it is set from the first vector indexed, which is a classic way to lock in the wrong size.

cards.prompt: Roughly how much raw memory do 10 million float32 vectors of 1,024 dimensions need, before any graph overhead or quantization?
options: 4 GB
10 GB
40 GB
400 GB
cards.why: 1,024 dims times 4 bytes is 4 KB per vector; times 10 million is about 40 GB. That number is why int8 (4x smaller) and BBQ (~32x smaller) quantization matter for a 2-million-document corpus.

cards.prompt: In Elasticsearch 9.1 and later, what is the default index_options type for a 1,024-dimension float dense_vector?
options: hnsw
int8_hnsw
bbq_hnsw
flat
cards.why: From 9.1, fields with 384 or more dimensions default to bbq_hnsw (binary quantization, about 32x smaller) and smaller fields to int8_hnsw. From 8.14 through 9.0 the default was int8_hnsw for all float vectors, which is what many candidates still quote.

cards.prompt: When an amended version of one contract is uploaded, the entire corpus must be re-embedded to keep the index consistent.
cards.why: Embeddings are per chunk and independent of other documents, so only the changed document's chunks are re-embedded and upserted. Full re-embedding is needed only when the model, its version or the chunking strategy changes.

cards.prompt: Cohere Embed v4 outputs ___ dimensions by default.
cards.why: Embed v4 defaults to 1,536 and lets you request 256, 512 or 1,024 instead, with a 128k-token context and multimodal input. Knowing the defaults matters because dims is baked into the index mapping.

explain.prompt: How do you roll out a new embedding model to a live index without downtime or mixed results?
explain.modelAnswer: The rule is that queries and documents must share a model, so I never mutate the live index in place. I treat it as a blue/green reindex, exactly like an Elasticsearch mapping change. First, create a new index with the new dims and quantization settings and an embed_model field recording the model id. Second, re-embed the whole corpus into it from the source documents, not from old vectors, in a batch job that is idempotent on document id plus content hash, so it can resume. Meanwhile the live alias still points at the old index and the old query path still uses the old model. Third, run the golden set against both indexes, each with its own query model, and compare recall@k and faithfulness; a new model is not automatically better on legal text. Fourth, flip the alias and the query-side model id in the same deploy, ideally behind a feature flag per client. Keep the old index for a week for rollback. Cost-wise, 10 million chunks through Titan V2 is a known embedding bill and a few hours of batch time, so this is routine rather than scary.
rubric: Never mix models in one index; build a second index
Re-embed from source documents, idempotent batch
Compare old vs new on a golden set before switching
Atomic cut-over of alias and query model together
Rollback path and cost estimate

scenarios.situation: A Fortune 100 legal department's RAG platform holds 12 million chunks as 1,024-dim float32 vectors on OpenSearch Serverless. The monthly bill is three times what finance approved, and most of it is vector-index capacity. The GC's office wants the cost halved within a quarter without hurting answer quality.
scenarios.question: What is your plan?

options.text: Measure recall@10 on the golden set at 1,024 vs 512 dimensions and with int8/binary quantization, pick the smallest configuration that stays within a point of baseline, and rebuild the index blue/green with that setting.
options.why: Titan V2 at 512 dims keeps about 99% of retrieval accuracy and halves storage; quantization cuts it further. Doing it against the golden set makes 'without hurting quality' a measurement, and blue/green keeps the live system untouched until proven.

options.text: Move archived matters' vectors to Amazon S3 Vectors, which is far cheaper per vector, and keep only active matters in OpenSearch.
options.why: S3 Vectors (GA December 2025) is a legitimate cold tier at up to 90% lower cost, but it has higher query latency and limits on hierarchical chunking and filters, and it adds a second query path to maintain. Good as a second step after shrinking the hot index.

options.text: Disable the vector index and serve answers from BM25 only, since the keyword index is cheap and lawyers know how to phrase searches.
options.why: You would meet the cost target by removing the capability the platform was bought for: paraphrase and concept questions. Quality would collapse on exactly the questions the GC's team asks.

nodes.title: Evaluating RAG
nodes.tease: The demo looked perfect. The golden set said 61% faithful. Which one do you believe?

primer.problem: A demo shows the five questions that worked. Before a firm trusts the assistant with client work, you need a number: how often is it right, and when it is wrong, did search fetch the wrong passages or did the model misuse the right ones? Without that split you fix the wrong thing.
primer.picture: Treat it like a test suite in an Azure DevOps pipeline. The **golden set** is the fixtures: real lawyer questions, each with the correct passages and a short reference answer. Search is tested like a plain function: did a correct passage come back in the top k? An answer can't be checked with `Assert.AreEqual`, so a second model, the **judge**, grades it against a rubric. Run both on every change and fail the build on regressions. The judge has its own biases, so compare it with lawyers' grades first.
primer.sketch:
golden question --> your pipeline --> retrieved chunks --> answer
                                          |                  |
      known correct chunks ---> recall@k  |                  |
                                (no model)  +--> judge model --+--> faithfulness,
                                                                  relevancy

terms.def: The share of questions where at least one known-correct passage appears in the top k search results.
An open-source Python library that scores RAG answers using a judge model, with metrics such as faithfulness and relevancy.
The share of claims in an answer that the retrieved passages actually support, from 0 to 1.
How directly the answer addresses the question asked, regardless of whether its facts are correct.
Whether the retrieved passages contain what is needed to support the reference answer; it needs a written reference answer.
Using a model to grade another model's output; it tends to favour the first answer shown, longer answers and its own style.
Pointwise grades one answer against a rubric; pairwise asks which of two answers is better, which invites position bias.

inPractice.setting: An HR-software SaaS whose help assistant answers 20,000 admin questions a week
inPractice.story:
The help assistant launched on the strength of a demo, and a month later the support team's verdict was 'sometimes wrong'. Product wanted to swap in a larger model. The tech lead asked for a number first.

Two senior support agents spent three days building a **golden set** of 150 questions from real tickets: single-article lookups, multi-article synthesis, payroll date arithmetic, and 20 unanswerable questions where the right reply is 'not in our docs'. Each row has the correct chunks and a short reference answer. Retrieval is scored with plain **recall@5**, no model involved. Generation is scored with RAGAS `Faithfulness` and `AnswerRelevancy` from `ragas.metrics.collections`, on the chunks the pipeline actually retrieved.

The numbers blamed retrieval: recall@5 was 0.71, while faithfulness on questions where the right chunk was present sat at 0.93. A bigger model would have fixed almost nothing; re-chunking the release notes lifted recall to 0.88.

The judge bit them once. It came from the same model family as the generator, and on a 60-item sample its grades ran consistently kinder than the agents', a textbook case of **self-preference**. A judge from another family brought agreement in line. The suite now runs in the deploy pipeline on every prompt or index change, fails the build on a two-point drop, and every escalated ticket becomes a new golden question.
inPractice.flow:
golden question -> pipeline.retrieve -> chunks -> pipeline.answer
  chunks vs labelled chunks -> recall@5                (no LLM)
  answer + chunks -> judge (other family) -> faithfulness, relevancy
  CI: fail build if metric < baseline - 0.02
inPractice.takeaway: I score retrieval and generation separately on a user-written golden set, calibrate the judge against human grades, and gate every deploy on regressions.

lesson.body:
You cannot improve what you only measure with a demo. A RAG evaluation separates the two things that can fail. **Retrieval** is scored against labelled relevant chunks with plain IR metrics: recall@k (did a relevant chunk appear in the top k), precision@k, MRR, nDCG. No LLM is involved, so it is fast, cheap and deterministic, and it tells you whether to fix chunking and search or the prompt. **Generation** is scored on the chunks the system actually retrieved.

RAGAS names the standard generation metrics (in the current `ragas.metrics.collections` API: `Faithfulness`, `AnswerRelevancy`, `ContextPrecision`, `ContextRecall`; the older `ragas.metrics` classes such as `ResponseRelevancy` still work but are slated for removal). *Faithfulness* decomposes the answer into claims and asks a judge whether each is supported by the retrieved context; the score is supported claims over total claims, 0 to 1. *Response relevancy* has the judge write N questions (default 3) that the answer would answer, embeds them, and averages cosine similarity to the real question, so padding and evasion score low. *Context precision* checks that relevant chunks rank above irrelevant ones; *context recall* needs a reference answer and checks whether the retrieved context could support it.

The judge is itself a model and inherits the biases documented by Zheng et al. (2023): position bias (prefers the first candidate), verbosity bias (longer looks better), self-preference (prefers its own family's style). Mitigate with pointwise rubrics instead of pairwise comparison, swapped orderings when you must compare, a judge from a different model family than the generator, and calibration: have lawyers grade 50-100 items and report agreement with the judge before you trust its numbers.

The **golden set** is the asset. Start with 100-200 questions written by the people who will use the system, stratified by type: single-clause lookup, cross-document synthesis, date arithmetic, and unanswerable questions where the right answer is 'not in these documents'. Version it, run it in CI on every prompt or index change, gate deploys on regressions, and feed every production failure back into it.
lesson.snippet:
from ragas import evaluate, EvaluationDataset
# legacy metric classes: still supported, deprecated in ragas 0.4, removed in 1.0.
# new code: from ragas.metrics.collections import Faithfulness, AnswerRelevancy, ContextRecall, ContextPrecision
from ragas.metrics import Faithfulness, ResponseRelevancy, LLMContextRecall, LLMContextPrecisionWithReference

# one row per golden question; retrieved_contexts come from YOUR pipeline, not hand-picked
rows = [{
    "user_input": "Does the liability cap apply to confidentiality breaches?",
    "retrieved_contexts": [c.text for c in pipeline.retrieve(q, user=test_lawyer)],
    "response": pipeline.answer(q, user=test_lawyer).text,
    "reference": "No. Section 12.3 excludes breaches of Section 9 from the cap.",
} for q in golden_set]

result = evaluate(
    EvaluationDataset.from_list(rows),
    metrics=[Faithfulness(), ResponseRelevancy(), LLMContextRecall(), LLMContextPrecisionWithReference()],
    llm=judge_llm,            # a different model family than the generator
    embeddings=judge_embeddings,
)
df = result.to_pandas()
assert df["faithfulness"].mean() >= BASELINE_FAITHFULNESS - 0.02   # CI gate
assert df["context_recall"].mean() >= BASELINE_RECALL - 0.02

cards.prompt: How does RAGAS compute Faithfulness?
options: Cosine similarity between the answer and the retrieved context
Number of answer claims supported by the retrieved context divided by total claims
Fraction of retrieved chunks that are quoted in the answer
A single 1-10 rating from the judge model
cards.why: The answer is decomposed into atomic claims and each is checked against the context; 3 of 4 supported gives 0.75. Cosine similarity would reward an answer that paraphrases the context without being correct about the question.

cards.prompt: How does RAGAS Response Relevancy work?
options: The judge rates whether the answer is relevant on a 0-1 scale
The judge generates N questions (default 3) the answer would answer, and their embeddings are compared by cosine similarity to the original question
It counts keyword overlap between the question and the answer
It checks whether the answer cites at least one retrieved chunk
cards.why: Reverse-engineering questions from the answer and averaging their similarity to the real question penalises answers that wander, pad or dodge. It needs an embedding model as well as a judge, and it says nothing about factual accuracy.

cards.prompt: Context recall can be computed from the question and retrieved chunks alone, without a reference answer.
cards.why: Context recall asks whether the retrieved context could support the reference answer, so it requires the reference. Faithfulness and response relevancy are the reference-free metrics; that is why they are cheap to run on production traffic.

cards.prompt: A judge model that systematically prefers whichever answer is shown first exhibits ___ bias.
cards.why: Documented in Zheng et al. (2023) along with verbosity and self-preference bias. The fix for pairwise judging is to evaluate both orderings and count a win only if it holds in both.

cards.prompt: Which metric isolates retriever quality and needs no LLM at all?
options: Faithfulness
Response relevancy
recall@k against labelled relevant chunks
Answer correctness
cards.why: Given a golden set that names which chunks are relevant, recall@k is a set intersection: deterministic, free and fast enough for every commit. The LLM-based metrics evaluate generation and cost money per run.

cards.prompt: A system scores 0.95 faithfulness but 0.40 response relevancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: The model is hallucinating facts not in the context
The model sticks to the retrieved context but is not answering the question that was asked
The retriever returned no documents
The judge model is broken
cards.why: High faithfulness means every claim is grounded; low relevancy means those grounded claims do not address the question, typically because retrieval brought back adjacent but wrong passages. Hallucination would show as low faithfulness.

cards.prompt: Using the same model as both generator and judge is best practice because it understands the task it was given.
cards.why: Models show self-preference bias, rating their own style higher. Use a judge from a different family, or at least a stronger model, and calibrate it against human labels before trusting the numbers.

cards.prompt: A golden set should include ___ questions, whose correct answer is 'not in these documents', to measure whether the system knows when to abstain.
cards.why: Without them a system that always produces a confident answer scores perfectly on faithfulness-style metrics while being dangerous in practice. Abstention rate on unanswerable questions is a first-class metric for legal work.

explain.prompt: You have zero labelled data on day one. How do you build an evaluation set for a legal Q&A system?
explain.modelAnswer: I start with the people who will use it. In the first week I sit with two or three associates and collect 100 to 150 real questions they would ask over a known matter, and for each one they point me at the clause or email that answers it and write a one-line reference answer. That gives me labelled relevant chunks for recall@k and a reference for context recall and correctness. I stratify deliberately: single-clause lookups, questions that span documents, date and amount questions, and about 15% unanswerable ones so I can measure abstention. To widen coverage cheaply I generate synthetic questions from randomly sampled chunks with a model, then have a lawyer skim and delete the silly ones; the generating chunk is the label. I version the set in git next to the code, run retrieval metrics on every commit and the LLM-judged metrics nightly, and record a baseline before any tuning. From go-live, every thumbs-down and every corrected answer becomes a new row, so the set grows from real failures rather than my imagination.
rubric: Domain experts write real questions with reference chunks and answers
Stratified by question type including unanswerable
Synthetic questions from chunks, human-filtered
Versioned and run in CI with a recorded baseline
Production failures feed back into the set

explain.prompt: What are the failure modes of LLM-as-a-judge, and how do you keep the judge honest?
explain.modelAnswer: A judge is another model with its own biases, so I treat its output as a measurement instrument that needs calibration. The known failures: position bias, where in pairwise comparisons the first answer wins more often; verbosity bias, where longer answers look more thorough; self-preference, where a model rates its own family's style higher; and rubric drift, where a vague 'rate 1-10' prompt gives inconsistent numbers. Mitigations: prefer pointwise scoring against an explicit rubric, for example faithfulness as supported claims over total claims, because it is more stable than pairwise; when I must compare, run both orderings and count a win only if it survives the swap; use a judge from a different family and ideally a stronger tier than the generator; pin the judge model version so scores are comparable over time; and most importantly calibrate, having lawyers grade 50 to 100 items and reporting agreement with the judge. If agreement is poor, the metric is noise and I fix the rubric before trusting any trend. I also spot-check judge explanations, because a judge that says 'supported' while citing nothing is as bad as a hallucinating generator.
rubric: Names position, verbosity and self-preference bias
Pointwise rubric preferred; swap orderings for pairwise
Judge from a different family and pinned version
Calibration against human-graded sample
Treats judge output as an instrument, not truth

scenarios.situation: Two weeks before go-live, a partner says the assistant's answers are 'sometimes wrong' but cannot say how often or which kind. The team has no evaluation set, 30 saved chat logs, and a proposal from one engineer to switch to a larger model to 'make it smarter'.
scenarios.question: What do you do with the two weeks?

options.text: Spend the first three days building a 120-question golden set with two associates from the 30 logs plus their own questions, run recall@k and faithfulness, and fix whichever stage the numbers blame before touching the model.
options.why: Without measurement you cannot tell retrieval failures from generation failures, and most 'wrong answers' are retrieval. The golden set also gives the partner a number to track instead of a feeling, and becomes the regression suite for every later change.

options.text: Add a self-verification step where the model re-reads the retrieved chunks and revises its answer before responding.
options.why: Self-checks do reduce some hallucinations and are cheap to add, but they double generation cost and do nothing if the right chunk was never retrieved. Worth trying, but only after you can measure whether it helped.

options.text: Switch to the largest available model for the remaining two weeks and ask the partner whether it feels better.
options.why: A bigger model cannot answer from a chunk it never received, costs several times more per answer, and 'feels better' is not evidence. You would go live blind with a higher bill.

nodes.title: Tracing Agents
nodes.tease: A $4,000 Bedrock bill from one weekend. Which tool call looped? Without traces you will never know.

primer.problem: An agent answers one question by calling search, the model and other tools, sometimes dozens of times. When an answer is wrong or a weekend bill hits $4,000, you need to see which step did what, how long it took and how many tokens it used, without copying privileged client text into a logging system.
primer.picture: It is distributed tracing, the correlation-id idea you know from Application Insights, applied to an agent. One user request is the root **span**; each retrieval, model call and tool call is a child span carrying timings, token counts and ids. The tree tells you whether the filter excluded the right matter or a tool looped 40 times. **OpenTelemetry** supplies the standard attribute names, such as `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, and a backend such as LangSmith or CloudWatch (AWS's monitoring service) stores the trees and draws them.
primer.sketch:
rag.answer (root span, 3.2 s)
|-- retrieve opensearch   180 ms   chunk_ids=[...]  filter=[matters]
|-- rerank                 90 ms
|-- chat claude          2.8 s    in=6,100 tok  out=420 tok
`-- tool: fetch_doc       120 ms

terms.def: The full record of one request as a tree of timed steps, linked by a shared trace id.
One timed step inside a trace, such as a single model call, with attributes like tokens used and latency.
The word-piece unit models read and write; providers bill per input and output token, so tokens equal cost.
The vendor-neutral open standard and SDKs for emitting traces, metrics and logs to any monitoring backend.
OpenTelemetry's agreed attribute names for model calls, like gen_ai.request.model; still at Development status, not Stable, so names can change.
LangChain's hosted tracing and evaluation service that shows each agent run as a browsable tree.
AWS's agent tracing view inside CloudWatch, which accepts OpenTelemetry spans from agents hosted anywhere.

inPractice.setting: A Berlin neobank's support agent handling 8,000 customer chats a day on ECS
inPractice.story:
The bank's support agent answers card and transfer questions by calling a transactions tool, a policy search and Claude on Bedrock, sometimes a dozen calls per chat. One Monday the team found a weekend Bedrock bill four times the usual, and logs that said only 'request completed'.

They instrumented the agent with OpenTelemetry. Each chat is a root **span**; children cover the policy search (filters, k, chunk ids), each model call with `gen_ai.request.model` and `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`/`output_tokens`, and each tool call. Chats contain account details, so `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT` stays unset: spans carry ids and counts, never text. After a one-time enable of CloudWatch Transaction Search, the ADOT SDK ships spans from ECS in eu-central-1 to CloudWatch's OTLP endpoint with SigV4, and they appear in **AgentCore Observability**.

The first trace tree explained the bill. When the transactions API returned a paging token, the agent kept calling the tool with the same token: 40 identical tool spans in one session. A loop cap fixed it, and an alarm on span count per session now fires before the invoice does.

One snag: a dependency bump replaced `gen_ai.system` with `gen_ai.provider.name` and broke a cost dashboard. Because the **GenAI semantic conventions** are still at Development stability, they now pin instrumentation versions.
inPractice.flow:
chat (root span)
|-- retrieve policy-search   chunk_ids=[...]  (no text)
|-- chat anthropic.claude    in/out tokens
`-- tool: get_transactions   x40  (the loop)
ADOT SDK -> CloudWatch OTLP endpoint (SigV4, eu-central-1)
  -> GenAI Observability page + alarm on spans per session
inPractice.takeaway: I trace every agent run as a span tree with OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes, keep message-content capture off for sensitive data, and alert on cost and span count per session.

lesson.body:
An agent run is a tree, and a trace is that tree with timings and payloads. The root span is the user request; children are retrieval (query text, filters, k, latency, returned chunk ids), rerank, each LLM call (model, input and output tokens, finish reason, latency) and each tool call. With that, 'why was this answer wrong' becomes 'the filter excluded the right matter' or 'the model ignored chunk 4', and 'why did the bill triple' becomes 'this tool looped 40 times per session'. It is the same discipline as correlation ids across services in Application Insights, applied to tokens.

The vendor-neutral vocabulary is the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions: `gen_ai.operation.name`, `gen_ai.provider.name` (which replaced `gen_ai.system`), `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.response.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`, with span names like `chat anthropic.claude-...`. They are still at Development stability, and in 2026 they moved out of the core semantic-conventions repository into a dedicated `semantic-conventions-genai` repository that had no tagged release as of autumn 2026, so pin instrumentation versions and expect renames. Prompt and completion text is opt-in through `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT`, which matters enormously when prompts contain privileged documents: keep it off by default and decide deliberately where that text may be stored and for how long.

**LangSmith** needs `LANGSMITH_TRACING=true`, `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` and `LANGSMITH_PROJECT`; decorate functions with `@traceable` or wrap the model client, and it also ingests OTel; EU tenants use `eu.api.smith.langchain.com`. Its datasets and `evaluate()` tie traces to the golden set. **AgentCore Observability** (GA 13 October 2025) renders agent traces in the CloudWatch GenAI Observability page after a one-time enable of CloudWatch Transaction Search; agents on AgentCore Runtime are auto-instrumented, others ship spans via the ADOT SDK to CloudWatch's OTLP endpoint with SigV4, so an ECS-hosted agent lands in the same dashboards. Emit cost per answer as a metric and alert on span count per session.
lesson.snippet:
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer("legal-assistant")

def answer(question: str, user: User) -> Answer:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("rag.answer") as root:
        root.set_attribute("app.matter_ids", user.permitted_matters)   # the filter actually used
        root.set_attribute("enduser.id", user.id)

        with tracer.start_as_current_span("retrieve opensearch") as s:
            s.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "retrieve")
            hits = search(question, filter=user.permitted_matters, k=50)
            s.set_attribute("app.chunk_ids", [h.id for h in hits])       # ids only, never text

        with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat anthropic.claude") as s:
            s.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")
            s.set_attribute("gen_ai.provider.name", "aws.bedrock")
            s.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", MODEL_ID)
            resp = bedrock_chat(prompt(question, hits[:8]))
            s.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", resp.usage.input_tokens)
            s.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", resp.usage.output_tokens)
            s.set_attribute("gen_ai.response.finish_reasons", [resp.stop_reason])
        # content capture stays off: OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT unset
        return resp

cards.prompt: Which OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute records the number of prompt tokens sent to the model?
options: gen_ai.request.tokens
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens
llm.prompt_tokens
gen_ai.prompt.length
cards.why: gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.output_tokens are the standard pair, and input tokens should include cached tokens. llm.prompt_tokens is an older vendor convention you will still see in some SDKs.

cards.prompt: As of 2026, the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions are marked Stable.
cards.why: Every gen_ai attribute, span and metric is still at Development stability, and in 2026 they moved to a dedicated semantic-conventions-genai repository that has not yet cut a tagged release. That is why you pin instrumentation versions and expect attribute renames such as gen_ai.system to gen_ai.provider.name.

cards.prompt: LangSmith tracing is switched on with the environment variable ___=true.
cards.why: Together with LANGSMITH_API_KEY and optionally LANGSMITH_PROJECT, that is the whole setup; @traceable or a wrapped client then records a run tree. EU tenants must also set LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT or authentication fails.

cards.prompt: Before AgentCore spans and traces appear in the CloudWatch GenAI Observability page, you must do a one-time enable of:
options: CloudWatch Container Insights
CloudWatch Transaction Search
AWS X-Ray sampling rules
Bedrock model invocation logging
cards.why: Transaction Search is the CloudWatch feature that indexes spans for the GenAI Observability views. Model invocation logging is separate and records prompts and completions, which is a privacy decision in its own right.

cards.prompt: Why should prompt and completion content capture be off by default in a law firm's agent telemetry?
options: It makes traces too slow to render
Prompts contain privileged client documents, so capturing them copies that text into the telemetry backend's retention and jurisdiction
OpenTelemetry does not support string attributes
LLM providers forbid logging their outputs
cards.why: A trace store is a second copy of client data with its own access controls, retention and possibly region. Record chunk ids, token counts and latencies by default; turn on content capture only for a scoped debugging window with approval.

cards.prompt: In newer OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, the attribute gen_ai.system was replaced by ___.
cards.why: The rename is one of several breaking changes while the conventions are in Development. Dashboards keyed on gen_ai.system silently go empty after an SDK upgrade.

cards.prompt: AgentCore Observability can only receive telemetry from agents that run on AgentCore Runtime.
cards.why: Agents on Runtime are auto-instrumented, but any agent instrumented with the ADOT SDK can send OTLP spans to CloudWatch's endpoint with SigV4, including ECS, on-premises or another cloud. Frameworks like Strands and LangChain already emit GenAI-convention spans.

explain.prompt: A client's Bedrock bill tripled last month and nobody changed the code. How do you find out why, and how do you stop it recurring?
explain.modelAnswer: First I go to the traces, because a bill is just the sum of gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and output_tokens across spans. I group spans by day and by operation to see whether the spike is more sessions, longer prompts, or more calls per session. Typical culprits: a tool-call loop where the agent retries the same failing tool dozens of times; a retrieval change that returns 50 chunks instead of 8 so every prompt is five times longer; a conversation history that is never trimmed; or a batch job someone pointed at production. The trace tree shows which: span count per session, prompt size per LLM span, and finish reasons. If I have no traces, that is finding number one. To prevent recurrence I emit cost per answer as a CloudWatch metric computed from token counts and model price, alert on spans per session and on daily spend per client, cap tool iterations in the agent loop, and put a hard budget in the agent framework. Then I add a cost assertion to the golden-set run so a prompt change that doubles tokens fails CI before it reaches the client.
rubric: Uses token attributes on spans to decompose the bill
Names concrete causes: loops, bigger prompts, untrimmed history
Diagnoses from span count and prompt size per session
Preventive metrics and alerts on cost and span count
Hard caps on iterations and a CI cost check

scenarios.situation: A Frankfurt-based law firm is deploying your agent on ECS in eu-central-1. The engineers want LangSmith for its debugging UI and have the default US endpoint and full prompt capture enabled in staging. The firm's DPO asks where client documents will be stored and under which jurisdiction.
scenarios.question: What do you set up for production?

options.text: Instrument with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, keep message-content capture off, record chunk ids and token counts, and ship spans to CloudWatch in eu-central-1 (or LangSmith's EU endpoint) after the DPO signs off on retention.
options.why: The trace store is a second copy of client data; keeping content off and the backend in-region answers the DPO's question truthfully. OTel keeps you vendor-neutral so the debugging UI choice is reversible.

options.text: Skip tracing in production and rely on structured application logs with request ids, adding traces only when a problem is reported.
options.why: Logs with correlation ids do answer some questions and avoid the data-residency issue, but you lose token accounting per span and the tree view that finds loops. You will be reconstructing traces by hand during the first incident.

options.text: Keep the staging configuration: LangSmith US endpoint with full prompt and completion capture, because it makes debugging fastest.
options.why: Privileged German client documents would be copied into a US-hosted store with its own retention. That is a GDPR and professional-secrecy problem the firm cannot accept, however good the UI.

nodes.title: Guardrails and Approval Gates
nodes.tease: The model 'approved' a settlement letter and sent it. Nobody asked a human. Where was the gate?

primer.problem: An agent can draft a letter, fill a privilege log or send an email. Models sometimes invent facts or take an action nobody approved, and a wrong letter sent to a client or filed with a court cannot be taken back. You need checks around the model that do not depend on the model behaving.
primer.picture: Treat the model as an untrusted API client. **Input checks** screen what goes in. **Output checks** validate what comes out, the way ASP.NET model binding plus FluentValidation rejects a bad request body, and a **grounding check** tests whether each claim is backed by the source passages. For anything irreversible, an **approval gate** works like a manual approval on an Azure DevOps environment: the workflow saves state, stops, and resumes only when a named human approves. None of these decide who may see a document; the search filter does that.
primer.sketch:
request -> input checks -> model drafts structured output
        -> schema validation -> grounding check vs retrieved chunks
        -> irreversible action?  no  -> do it
                                 yes -> save state, notify approver, STOP
                                        human approves -> resume

terms.def: Instructions hidden in a document or input that try to make the model ignore its real instructions.
Asking the model to answer as JSON matching a schema, so your code can validate fields before acting on them.
AWS's managed checks, such as content filters, denied topics, PII masking and grounding; its ApplyGuardrail API screens any model's text.
A score of whether every claim in an answer is supported by the source passages, and whether it answers the question.
A Bedrock Guardrails feature that turns a written policy into formal logic and proves a statement valid or invalid.
Personally identifiable information, such as names, addresses or account numbers, that must be masked or blocked.
The list a party must hand over describing each document it withholds as privileged: date, author, recipients and basis.

inPractice.setting: A freight forwarder's agent drafting delay notices for 400 shipping customers
inPractice.story:
When a vessel slipped its schedule, account managers spent hours writing delay emails. The team built an agent that reads the carrier's schedule update and the booking records, then drafts a notice per affected customer. In the pilot it wrote a polished email promising arrival on 14 March. No source said 14 March; the model had blended two dates.

They rebuilt the output path. The agent now returns **structured output** (booking id, old and new ETA, port, reason), validated server-side against a JSON schema before anything else happens. The draft then goes through `ApplyGuardrail` with the schedule update and booking record tagged `grounding_source`, the customer's question tagged `query`, and the draft as the guarded content. Its **contextual grounding check** uses thresholds of 0.85 for grounding and 0.5 for relevance, and anything that fails goes to an account manager instead of the outbox.

The trade-off was cost against coverage. Grounding checks bill per 1,000-character text unit, so the source is just the one booking and the relevant schedule update, not the whole carrier feed.

Sending stays behind an **approval gate**: the workflow checkpoints the batch, notifies the account manager, and resumes only on an explicit approval. In three months, no notice went out with a date its sources did not contain.
inPractice.flow:
schedule update + bookings -> agent -> JSON draft
  -> schema validation (server-side)
  -> ApplyGuardrail: grounding_source | query | draft
       below threshold -> account manager review
  -> checkpoint batch -> approval request -> STOP
       approved -> send emails
inPractice.takeaway: I never let the model gate itself: schema-validated output, a grounding check against the sources, and a human approval before any irreversible action like sending.

lesson.body:
Guardrails are layers, and none of them is the retrieval filter. **Input validation**: schema and length checks, allow-listed tools, prompt-injection detection on anything that came from a document rather than the user. **Output validation**: request structured output against a JSON schema and validate it server-side, the way ASP.NET model binding plus FluentValidation treats a request body; never let free text drive a side effect. **Human approval gates**: any irreversible or expensive action (send to a client, file with a court, delete, spend above a threshold) pauses the workflow, persists state, and resumes only on an explicit approval, like a manual approval on an Azure DevOps environment. An agent that 'asks itself' for permission has no gate.

**Amazon Bedrock Guardrails** adds managed policies you attach to Converse/Invoke or call directly through `ApplyGuardrail`, which works with any model including self-hosted ones. Policies: content filters (Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, Misconduct, Prompt Attack, each with a strength), denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters (PII entities or regex; block or mask), **contextual grounding checks**, and **Automated Reasoning checks** (GA 6 August 2025), which compile a written policy into formal logic and prove or refute statements instead of estimating a confidence. Grounding checks score grounding (is every claim supported by the source) and relevance (does it answer the query) against thresholds from 0 to 0.99; they run on the output only, and cap at 100,000 characters of source, 1,000 of query and 5,000 of response. With `ApplyGuardrail` you tag content blocks with `qualifiers`: `grounding_source` for the retrieved passages, `query`, and an unqualified or `guard_content` block for the answer. Billing is per policy per 1,000 text units of up to 1,000 characters each: content filters and denied topics $0.15, PII filters and grounding checks $0.10, Automated Reasoning $0.17 per policy; regex and word filters are free.

What guardrails do not do: decide who may see a document. A denied topic is not an ethical wall; that remains the retrieval-time permission filter.

resp = bedrock_runtime.apply_guardrail(
    guardrailIdentifier=GUARDRAIL_ID, guardrailVersion="3",
    source="OUTPUT",                      # grounding checks only run on output
    content=[
        {"text": {"text": "\n\n".join(c.text for c in retrieved_chunks),
                  "qualifiers": ["grounding_source"]}},     # <= 100,000 chars
        {"text": {"text": question, "qualifiers": ["query"]}},  # <= 1,000 chars
        {"text": {"text": draft_answer}},                      # content to guard, <= 5,000
    ],
)
if resp["action"] == "GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED":
    # inspect resp["assessments"][0]["contextualGroundingPolicy"]["filters"]
    # each filter has type GROUNDING | RELEVANCE, score, threshold, action
    return abstain("I could not ground an answer in the retrieved documents.")

# irreversible step: stop and wait for a human, do not let the model decide
if action.kind in {"send_to_client", "file_with_court"}:
    checkpoint.save(state)
    approvals.request(action, approver=supervising_partner)
    raise PausedForApproval(action.id)

source.title: Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses - Amazon Bedrock

cards.prompt: What range of threshold values does a Bedrock contextual grounding check accept for grounding and relevance?
options: 0 to 1 inclusive
cards.why: A threshold of 1 is rejected because it would block every response; 0.99 is the maximum. Responses whose grounding or relevance score falls below the threshold are treated as hallucinations and blocked or flagged.

cards.prompt: Bedrock's contextual grounding check evaluates the input prompt as well as the model's output.
cards.why: Grounding needs a response to compare against the source, so it only runs on output. Content filters, denied topics, word filters and PII filters are the policies that run on both input and output.

cards.prompt: Bedrock's ___ API lets you run a guardrail against any model's text, including self-hosted or third-party models that never touch Bedrock inference.
cards.why: ApplyGuardrail decouples the policy from the model, so one guardrail can govern a Bedrock model, an on-prem model and a vendor API consistently. It also means you can run grounding checks on a draft before any side effect.

cards.prompt: In an ApplyGuardrail call for a RAG answer, which qualifier marks the retrieved passages?
options: guard_content
query
grounding_source
context
cards.why: grounding_source is the reference the answer is checked against, query is the user's question, and the unqualified or guard_content block is the text being guarded. Content tagged grounding_source or query is excluded from the other policies unless you also add guard_content.

cards.prompt: What is the correct implementation of a human approval gate before an agent sends a letter to a client?
options: Add 'always ask the user before sending' to the system prompt
Have the model call an approve_self tool that returns true when it is confident
Persist the workflow state, stop execution, notify an approver, and resume only when an authenticated human approves
Send the letter and allow recall within 60 seconds
cards.why: A gate must be enforced by the orchestrator, not requested of the model. Checkpointing and resuming on approval is the same pattern as a manual approval stage on an Azure DevOps environment; a prompt instruction is optional by construction.

cards.prompt: A denied-topics policy in Bedrock Guardrails is an acceptable substitute for retrieval-time permission filters between matters.
cards.why: Topic filters classify what the text is about, not who may see it; two matters can share every topic. Access control has to happen before retrieval returns a chunk, and guardrails run after the text already exists.

cards.prompt: How do Automated Reasoning checks differ from contextual grounding checks?
options: They are the same feature under a new name
Automated Reasoning compiles a written policy into formal logic and proves or refutes statements; grounding uses an ML model to score confidence against a source
Automated Reasoning runs on input; grounding runs on output
Automated Reasoning only works with Amazon's own models
cards.why: Automated Reasoning (GA August 2025) encodes rules such as eligibility or approval policies as logic and returns findings like valid or invalid with explanations; grounding is a probabilistic check on whether claims are supported by retrieved text. They catch different errors and can be combined.

cards.prompt: The grounding source for a Bedrock contextual grounding check is limited to ___ characters.
cards.why: Source is capped at 100,000 characters, the query at 1,000 and the response at 5,000. For a 50-chunk prompt you will hit the source cap, which is another reason to rerank down to a handful of chunks before generation.

explain.prompt: Describe the guardrail layers you would put around an agent that drafts and sends client-facing letters.
explain.modelAnswer: I think in layers from the outside in. Input: the request is validated against a schema, the agent only has the tools this workflow needs, and anything retrieved from documents is treated as untrusted text and scanned for prompt injection before it reaches the model. Retrieval: the permission filter decides which documents it may draw from; no guardrail replaces that. Generation: the draft is produced as structured output against a JSON schema, recipient, matter id, body, cited chunk ids, and validated server-side like any API request body. Then a Bedrock contextual grounding check runs on the body with the retrieved chunks as grounding_source, PII filters mask anything that should not leave the firm, and I verify every cited id exists. The critical layer is the approval gate: 'send' is an irreversible action, so the orchestrator checkpoints the state, stops, and notifies the supervising lawyer; it resumes only on their authenticated approval, never on the model's say-so. Every step is traced with token counts and chunk ids for audit. The model drafts; humans and deterministic code decide.
rubric: Input validation and injection scanning of retrieved text
Structured output validated server-side
Grounding check and PII masking before the side effect
Orchestrator-enforced human approval with persisted state
Permission filter at retrieval is separate from guardrails
Audit trace of the whole run

scenarios.situation: An agent drafts privilege-log entries for a Fortune 100 client's document production: for each withheld document it writes the date, author, recipients, privilege basis and a description, then a tool uploads the log to the production platform. The deadline is Friday. A reviewer notices one entry described a document as 'draft board minutes' when it was an email, and the privilege basis was invented.
scenarios.question: What do you change before resuming?

options.text: Produce each entry as structured output validated against a schema, run a contextual grounding check of description and basis against the document's own text, route any entry below threshold to a reviewer, and gate the upload tool behind an explicit human approval of the batch.
options.why: An invented privilege basis can waive privilege or draw sanctions, so the side effect must sit behind deterministic checks and a human. Grounding and schema validation catch the fabrication; the approval gate makes the upload an attorney's act, not the model's.

options.text: Have a second model call review each entry and correct it before upload, keeping the upload automatic to hit Friday.
options.why: A reviewer model reduces errors and is cheap, but it is another probabilistic step with no accountability, and the upload remains unsupervised. It is a reasonable addition inside the gate, not a replacement for it.

options.text: Lower the model temperature, add 'never invent a privilege basis' to the prompt, and resume automated uploads.
options.why: Prompt instructions are suggestions, not controls, and temperature does not prevent fabrication. You would be producing a court-facing document with the same failure mode and no way to catch it.

questions.prompt: Design a system that lets lawyers ask questions over 2 million documents across hundreds of matters. Walk me through ingestion, indexing, retrieval, security, answer generation and how you would know it works.
questions.modelOutline: Start with constraints: per-matter confidentiality, ethical walls, citations that must be verifiable, EU data residency, and a budget. Ingestion: S3 landing, event-driven workers (Step Functions or Kafka consumers) that parse and OCR, dedupe by hash, extract metadata (matter, custodian, date, privilege) into sidecars, idempotent on doc id. Chunking: structure-aware, Article/Section boundaries with heading breadcrumbs and parent/child, email threads by message. Index: OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, hybrid BM25 plus kNN with quantized vectors, partitioned per matter or client, RRF fusion. Security: entitlements resolved server-side and applied as a pre-filter in every query, deny by default. Reranker over the top 50, keep eight. Generation with chunk ids, citations verified against retrieved ids, abstain when nothing grounds. Audit log of user, filter, chunk ids, tokens, model. Guardrails: grounding check, PII masking, approval gates for any action. Evaluation: golden set per matter type, recall@k and faithfulness in CI, cost per answer tracked in traces. Close with the rollout: pilot one matter, measure, expand.
rubric: Ingestion pipeline: parse/OCR, dedupe, metadata extraction, idempotent and event-driven
Structure-aware chunking with breadcrumbs and parent/child for legal documents
Per-matter (or per-client) hybrid index: BM25 plus kNN fused with RRF, quantized vectors
Permission filters derived server-side and applied as pre-filters, deny by default
Cross-encoder reranker over a shortlist before generation
Citations tied to chunk ids and verified; abstains when ungrounded
Audit log of user, filter, chunk ids, model and tokens per request
Golden evaluation set with retrieval and faithfulness metrics run in CI

questions.prompt: How do you know the agent's answers are good?
questions.modelOutline: Define 'good' as three measurable things: the right evidence was retrieved, the answer is faithful to that evidence and actually answers the question, and the system abstains when it should. Build a golden set with domain experts: 100-200 questions with labelled relevant chunks and reference answers, stratified by type including unanswerable. Measure retrieval with recall@k and nDCG, deterministic and free; measure generation with RAGAS-style faithfulness (supported claims over total), response relevancy, context recall. Use an LLM judge from a different family with pointwise rubrics, swapped orderings for comparisons, and calibrate it against lawyer grades before trusting it. Run the set in CI on every prompt, model or index change and gate deploys on regressions. In production, sample traces for judged faithfulness, track thumbs-down and corrected answers, feed them back into the set, and watch cost and latency per answer alongside quality.
rubric: Separates retrieval quality from generation quality
Golden set built with domain experts, stratified, includes unanswerable questions
Retrieval metrics (recall@k, nDCG) that need no LLM
Generation metrics: faithfulness, response relevancy, context recall
LLM-as-judge biases named and mitigated, calibrated against humans
Evaluation runs in CI and gates deploys
Production monitoring: sampled judging, user feedback loop, cost per answer
